questions.prompt: Which property of the Queue data structure ensures that BFS explores all nodes at distance 'k' before moving to distance 'k+1'?
options: Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) ensures we backtrack to the most recent node.
First-In, First-Out (FIFO) ensures nodes discovered earlier are processed first.
Random access allows the algorithm to jump between non-adjacent levels.
Priority-based sorting ensures the node with the lowest value is processed next.
questions.explanation: BFS uses a Queue because its FIFO property maintains the order of discovery. This ensures that every node at the current level is pulled out and processed before any nodes from the next level (added later) can reach the front of the queue.
correctAnswers: First-In, First-Out (FIFO) ensures nodes discovered earlier are processed first.

questions.prompt: In a graph with cycles, what are the primary purposes of maintaining a 'visited' set during a BFS traversal?
options: To prevent the algorithm from entering an infinite loop.
To ensure that each node's shortest distance from the source is only calculated once.
To store the final alphabetical order of the nodes in the graph.
To allow the algorithm to traverse back to the root once the target is found.
To avoid re-adding a node to the queue if it has already been discovered.
questions.explanation: A 'visited' set tracks which nodes have already been processed or added to the queue. Without it, a cycle would cause the algorithm to keep re-adding the same nodes indefinitely, and we would lose the guarantee that the first time we see a node is its shortest path.
correctAnswers: To prevent the algorithm from entering an infinite loop.
To ensure that each node's shortest distance from the source is only calculated once.
To avoid re-adding a node to the queue if it has already been discovered.

questions.prompt: In an unweighted graph, BFS is guaranteed to find the ____ path because it explores the graph in concentric layers outward from the source.
questions.explanation: Because BFS visits nodes level-by-level (distance 1, then distance 2, etc.), the first time it reaches a target node, it must be via the path with the fewest number of edges.
correctAnswers: shortest
minimum
optimal

questions.prompt: In a social network graph where edges represent 'friendship', how is the distance to a new node calculated during BFS?
options: It is the distance of the parent node minus 1.
It is always 1, regardless of the path taken.
It is the distance of the parent node plus 1.
It is calculated by summing the total number of nodes in the graph.
questions.explanation: Since BFS explores layer-by-layer, every time we discover a new node through a 'parent', that child node is exactly one step further from the source than the parent was.
correctAnswers: It is the distance of the parent node plus 1.

questions.prompt: Why does the discovery process spread in uniform 'ripples' rather than extending deep into one branch of the graph?
options: Because the Queue forces all neighbors of the current node to be added and processed before any of their own neighbors can be reached.
Because the graph is automatically sorted by edge weight before the search begins.
Because the algorithm uses a Stack, which prioritizes the oldest nodes in the network.
Because the 'visited' set restricts the search to only one direction at a time.
questions.explanation: The 'ripple' effect occurs because a Queue processes nodes in the order they were discovered. If Node A is at distance 1 and Node B is at distance 2, Node A must leave the Queue before Node B can even be processed.

questions.prompt: While tracing a DFS traversal on a graph with a cycle, you notice the algorithm has entered an infinite loop. Which implementation error is the most likely cause?
options: Using a Stack instead of a Queue to manage the nodes
Failing to mark a node as 'visited' before its recursive calls
Using a recursive approach instead of an iterative one
Starting the search from a node that is part of the cycle
questions.explanation: In a graph with cycles, DFS will revisit the same nodes repeatedly unless they are marked as 'visited'. Without this check, the algorithm will keep 'diving' into the same path forever.
correctAnswers: Failing to mark a node as 'visited' before its recursive calls

questions.prompt: A node in a DFS traversal is assigned an entry time of 3 and an exit time of 10. What can be definitively concluded about the nodes explored during this interval?
options: Any node with an entry time of 4 and exit time of 9 is a descendant of this node
All nodes visited between time 3 and 10 are at the same depth in the graph
The node was 'Visiting' (active on the stack) for exactly 7 time units
The search found a dead end exactly at time 5
The node remained on the call stack until all its reachable descendants were fully explored
questions.explanation: Entry and exit times define the 'lifetime' of a node on the stack. Any node explored within that window is a descendant, and the parent node cannot be 'finished' (popped) until all its children are 'Visited'.
correctAnswers: Any node with an entry time of 4 and exit time of 9 is a descendant of this node
The node remained on the call stack until all its reachable descendants were fully explored

questions.prompt: To transform a Breadth-First Search logic into a Depth-First Search logic, the underlying data structure must be changed from a Queue to a ____.
questions.explanation: BFS uses a Queue (FIFO) to explore level-by-level, while DFS uses a Stack (LIFO)—either explicitly or via the system's call stack—to explore as deep as possible.
correctAnswers: Stack
LIFO
LIFO buffer
Last-In-First-Out

questions.prompt: You are designing an AI to solve a maze where the solution is known to be very deep, but the maze itself is very narrow with few branching paths. Why might DFS be a risky choice here?
options: DFS will explore the width of the maze first, wasting time
The memory required for the Queue will exceed available RAM
The deep recursion might cause a Stack Overflow error
DFS is unable to find paths in narrow environments
questions.explanation: Because DFS goes as deep as possible before backtracking, a very deep path results in a very large call stack. In limited-memory environments, this can crash the program even if the graph isn't 'wide'.
correctAnswers: The deep recursion might cause a Stack Overflow error

questions.prompt: In which of the following scenarios is Depth-First Search generally more appropriate than Breadth-First Search?
options: Finding the shortest path in an unweighted social network
Detecting a cycle within a directed graph
Exhaustively searching all possible states in a puzzle to see if a solution exists
Finding the closest 'gas station' node to a starting 'car' node
Performing a topological sort based on entry and exit times
questions.explanation: DFS is the primary tool for exhaustive search and detecting cycles (via back-edges). BFS is superior for finding the shortest path or 'closest' items in unweighted graphs.
correctAnswers: Detecting a cycle within a directed graph
Exhaustively searching all possible states in a puzzle to see if a solution exists
Performing a topological sort based on entry and exit times

questions.prompt: In Kahn's Algorithm for topological sorting, what does it mean if the result list contains fewer nodes than the total number of vertices in the graph, even though the processing queue is empty?
options: The graph is disconnected but acyclic.
The graph contains at least one cycle.
The starting node was selected incorrectly.
The graph is a tree rather than a general DAG.
questions.explanation: Kahn's algorithm only processes nodes with an in-degree of zero. If a cycle exists, the nodes within that cycle will never have an in-degree of zero (even after their external dependencies are removed), causing the algorithm to terminate prematurely.
correctAnswers: The graph contains at least one cycle.

questions.prompt: Which of the following conditions must be true for a graph to have a valid topological sort?
options: The graph must be directed.
The graph must be connected.
The graph must not contain any cycles.
The graph must have at least one node with an in-degree of zero.
The graph must be a binary search tree.
questions.explanation: Topological sorting only applies to Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs). A DAG must have at least one 'source' (in-degree 0) to begin the sort, but it does not need to be fully connected (multiple components can each have their own sort).
correctAnswers: The graph must be directed.
The graph must not contain any cycles.
The graph must have at least one node with an in-degree of zero.

questions.prompt: When using three-color marking (White, Gray, Black) for cycle detection, why is encountering a 'Black' node considered safe, whereas encountering a 'Gray' node indicates a cycle?
options: A Black node has no outgoing edges, so it cannot be part of any path.
A Gray node is already in the current recursion stack, meaning a path exists from it back to itself.
Black nodes are only used in undirected graphs, while Gray nodes are used in DAGs.
The Black state indicates that the node is the 'sink' of the entire graph.
questions.explanation: Gray indicates a node that is 'in progress.' If you see a Gray node during a DFS, you have found a 'back edge' to an ancestor in the current search path, which completes a cycle. Black nodes are fully processed and do not lead back to the current path.
correctAnswers: A Gray node is already in the current recursion stack, meaning a path exists from it back to itself.

questions.prompt: Based on the simulation of Kahn's Algorithm, why does the number of available nodes in the 'Ready Queue' fluctuate rather than just steadily decreasing?
options: Because removing a node can 'unlock' multiple children by reducing their in-degree to zero.
Because nodes are re-added to the queue if their dependencies fail to compile.
Because the algorithm prioritizes nodes with the highest number of outgoing edges first.
Because the queue only holds nodes that are part of a detected cycle.
questions.explanation: As the simulation shows, the queue grows when a processed node was the final dependency for several neighbors, making them 'ready.' It shrinks as those nodes are pulled out for the final sort list.

correctAnswers: Because removing a node can 'unlock' multiple children by reducing their in-degree to zero.

questions.prompt: In the context of Dijkstra's algorithm, what does it mean to 'relax' an edge between two nodes, U and V?
options: Checking if the path to V through U is shorter than the currently known path to V and updating it if so.
Removing the edge from the graph once the algorithm determines it is not part of the shortest path.
Reducing the weight of an edge to zero to prioritize that specific path in the next iteration.
Marking node V as 'visited' regardless of the distance calculated from node U.
questions.explanation: Relaxation is the process of updating the cost to reach a neighbor. If the distance to node U plus the weight of the edge (U, V) is less than the current best distance to V, we 'relax' the constraint and update V's distance.
correctAnswers: Checking if the path to V through U is shorter than the currently known path to V and updating it if so.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are necessary conditions or components for Dijkstra's algorithm to successfully find the shortest path in its standard O((E+V) log V) implementation?
options: All edge weights must be non-negative.
A priority queue (Min-Heap) must be used to select the next node.
The graph must be a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG).
Initial distances to all nodes except the source must be set to infinity.
The graph must contain at least one negative cycle.
questions.explanation: Dijkstra requires non-negative weights because it assumes once a node is finalized, its distance cannot decrease. A Min-Heap is required for the O(log V) efficiency, and starting distances must be infinity to represent initial ignorance.
correctAnswers: All edge weights must be non-negative.
A priority queue (Min-Heap) must be used to select the next node.
Initial distances to all nodes except the source must be set to infinity.

questions.prompt: If a graph has V vertices and E edges, using a binary heap to implement Dijkstra's algorithm results in a time complexity of ____.
correctAnswers: O((E+V) log V)
O(E log V)
(E+V)logV

questions.prompt: When executing Dijkstra's algorithm, why do we use a priority queue instead of a standard unsorted list to store tentative distances?
options: To ensure we always process the node with the current minimum tentative distance in logarithmic time.
To keep the edges sorted by their original weights before the algorithm starts.
To allow the algorithm to handle negative edge weights automatically.
To store the history of all paths explored to prevent visiting the same node twice.
questions.explanation: A priority queue (Min-Heap) allows us to extract the node with the minimum distance in O(log V) time. Without it, we would have to scan all nodes to find the minimum, which would take O(V) time per extraction.
correctAnswers: To ensure we always process the node with the current minimum tentative distance in logarithmic time.

questions.prompt: Why does the algorithm fail to find the correct shortest path to the final node in this simulation?
options: The presence of a negative weight edge allows a later path to 'undercut' a node that was already finalized.
The algorithm mistakenly picks the node with the largest distance instead of the smallest distance.
The priority queue cannot handle graphs that contain cycles, causing an infinite loop.
The relaxation step only updates the neighbors of the source node instead of all adjacent nodes.
questions.explanation: Dijkstra is a greedy algorithm that assumes once a node's shortest path is found and 'settled', it never needs to be updated. A negative edge can make a longer path suddenly much cheaper, breaking this fundamental assumption.

questions.prompt: Why does the Bellman-Ford algorithm perform exactly V-1 iterations of edge relaxation to guarantee shortest paths in a graph without negative cycles?
options: Because any simple path in a graph with V vertices can contain at most V-1 edges.
Because V-1 is the average number of edges connected to the source node.
Because it takes V-1 iterations to reach the maximum weight limit of an integer.
Because the algorithm must visit every edge exactly once to ensure efficiency.
questions.explanation: In a graph with V vertices, the longest possible path that does not visit the same node twice (a simple path) has V-1 edges. Since each iteration of Bellman-Ford relaxes all edges, it essentially extends the known shortest paths by one edge per iteration, reaching any possible node by the (V-1)th pass.
correctAnswers: Because any simple path in a graph with V vertices can contain at most V-1 edges.

questions.prompt: Which of the following scenarios would make Bellman-Ford a more appropriate choice than Dijkstra's algorithm?
options: The graph contains negative edge weights but no negative cycles.
The system needs to detect 'infinite arbitrage' opportunities in currency exchange.
The graph is extremely large (1 million+ nodes) and all weights are positive.
The graph is a DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) with only positive weights.
questions.explanation: Bellman-Ford is necessary when negative weights are present because Dijkstra's greedy approach fails. It is also the standard method for detecting negative cycles (arbitrage), whereas Dijkstra cannot handle negative values at all.
correctAnswers: The graph contains negative edge weights but no negative cycles.
The system needs to detect 'infinite arbitrage' opportunities in currency exchange.

questions.prompt: If a distance to any node is successfully relaxed during the ____ iteration of the Bellman-Ford algorithm, it serves as mathematical proof that a negative cycle exists in the graph.
questions.explanation: After V-1 iterations, all shortest paths should be found. If a V-th iteration still results in a path distance decreasing, it means a cycle with a negative sum is allowing the path to infinitely decrease in weight.
correctAnswers: Vth
V
V-th
last
extra

questions.prompt: What is the primary reason Dijkstra's algorithm is preferred over Bellman-Ford for graphs where all edge weights are known to be positive?
options: Dijkstra has a superior time complexity of O((V+E) log V) compared to O(V*E).
Bellman-Ford cannot find the shortest path if all edges are positive.
Dijkstra's algorithm is easier to implement without using arrays.
Bellman-Ford requires more memory to store the graph's edge list.
questions.explanation: Dijkstra's algorithm is significantly faster (logarithmic vs linear scaling per vertex). For a graph with 1,000 nodes and 10,000 edges, Bellman-Ford does 10 million operations while Dijkstra does far fewer.
correctAnswers: Dijkstra has a superior time complexity of O((V+E) log V) compared to O(V*E).

questions.prompt: As the iterations of the algorithm progress, why do some node values remain at infinity for several steps before suddenly dropping to a finite number?

The algorithm intentionally waits for the negative weights to be processed last.
The node is part of a negative cycle that hasn't been closed yet.
The edge weights are being updated in reverse alphabetical order.
questions.explanation: In each iteration 'i', Bellman-Ford finds the shortest path to nodes that are at most 'i' edges away from the source. A node requiring 3 edges to reach will remain at infinity during iterations 1 and 2.

questions.prompt: How does the core objective of a Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) differ from the objective of Dijkstra's algorithm for Shortest Paths?
options: The MST seeks to minimize the total weight of all edges in the connected set, while Dijkstra's seeks to minimize the distance from a source to every other node.
The MST focuses on reaching the furthest node in the fewest number of hops, while Dijkstra's focuses on edge weights.
Dijkstra's algorithm ensures there are no cycles in the resulting graph, whereas an MST may contain multiple redundant loops.
An MST always selects the heaviest edges to ensure connectivity, while Dijkstra's always selects the lightest.
questions.explanation: MST focuses on the global cost of connecting every node in a network (infrastructure optimization), whereas Dijkstra's optimizes the specific path distance from a single starting point to others (navigation optimization).
correctAnswers: The MST seeks to minimize the total weight of all edges in the connected set, while Dijkstra's seeks to minimize the distance from a source to every other node.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements accurately describe the behavior of Kruskal’s algorithm?
options: It maintains a single growing tree structure throughout the entire execution.
It treats the graph as a forest of trees that gradually merge into one.
It requires all edges to be sorted by weight before the selection process begins.
It will always produce the exact same set of edges as Prim's algorithm, even if there are ties in edge weights.
questions.explanation: Kruskal's starts with every node as its own tree and merges them by choosing the lightest available edge that doesn't cause a cycle. If there are duplicate weights, different algorithms might pick different edges, leading to different but valid MSTs.
correctAnswers: It treats the graph as a forest of trees that gradually merge into one.
It requires all edges to be sorted by weight before the selection process begins.

questions.prompt: In MST algorithms, the critical rule that must be followed to ensure the result is a tree and not just a subgraph is to never create a ____.
questions.explanation: A tree, by definition, is a connected graph with no cycles. If an algorithm adds an edge that connects two nodes already in the same component, it creates a redundant path (cycle), which violates the spanning tree property.
correctAnswers: cycle
loop
closed path

questions.prompt: If a graph contains multiple edges with the same minimum weight, how does this affect the outcome of MST algorithms?
options: The algorithms will fail to converge on a solution.
The MST for that graph may not be unique.
The total weight of the MST will increase.
Kruskal's will work, but Prim's will produce an invalid tree.
questions.explanation: When ties in edge weights occur, the order of selection might differ depending on the implementation or algorithm used. This can result in different sets of edges that both satisfy the 'minimum' weight requirement.
correctAnswers: The MST for that graph may not be unique.

questions.prompt: Observe the growth of the spanning tree. Why does the algorithm pass over the edge with weight 4 even though it is cheaper than the edge with weight 10 selected later?
options: The weight 4 edge would have connected two nodes already belonging to the same tree component, forming a cycle.
The algorithm is Prim's, and the weight 4 edge was not connected to the current starting node's branch.
The weight 4 edge was part of a disconnected component that the algorithm cannot reach.
The algorithm prioritize edges that connect to the highest-degree nodes first.
questions.explanation: In Kruskal's, edges are considered in order of weight, but if the two endpoints of an edge are already connected via other edges, adding it would create a cycle. This is why a light edge can be rejected in favor of a heavier one that connects a new part of the graph.

questions.prompt: In a Disjoint Set Union (DSU) data structure, why do we use 'Path Compression' during the find operation?
options: To ensure that every node in the set is immediately deleted after it is found
To flatten the tree structure by making traversed nodes point directly to the root
To increase the rank of the tree every time a search is performed
To allow a single node to belong to multiple different sets simultaneously
questions.explanation: Path compression optimizes future operations by shortening the path to the root. As we traverse up the tree to find the 'captain' (root), we update each visited node's parent pointer to point directly to that root, preventing long, inefficient chains.
correctAnswers: To flatten the tree structure by making traversed nodes point directly to the root

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements accurately describe the 'Union by Rank' heuristic?
options: It always attaches the root of the tree with the smaller rank to the root of the tree with the larger rank.
It ensures that the height of the resulting tree only increases if the ranks of the two trees being joined are equal.
It guarantees that the find operation will always take O(1) time regardless of path compression.
The 'rank' value acts as an upper bound on the height of the tree.
It requires merging the larger tree into the smaller tree to maintain balance.
questions.explanation: Union by Rank keeps trees 'bushy' and short. If we merge two trees of different ranks, the taller one remains the root and the height doesn't change; height only increases (by 1) if we merge two trees of the same rank. Rank is an upper bound because path compression might actually make the tree shorter than its rank suggests.
correctAnswers: It always attaches the root of the tree with the smaller rank to the root of the tree with the larger rank.
It ensures that the height of the resulting tree only increases if the ranks of the two trees being joined are equal.
The 'rank' value acts as an upper bound on the height of the tree.

questions.prompt: In the 'Union by Rank' strategy, if two trees with rank 3 and rank 5 are merged, the rank of the new root will be ____.
In the context of Kruskal's algorithm, what is the primary purpose of the 'Find' operation?
options: To sort the edges of the graph by their weight in ascending order
To determine if adding an edge between two vertices would create a cycle
To calculate the total weight of the Minimum Spanning Tree
To remove redundant vertices from the graph before processing edges
questions.explanation: If Find(u) and Find(v) return the same root, it means u and v are already in the same connected component. Adding an edge between them would create a cycle, which Kruskal's algorithm must avoid.
correctAnswers: To determine if adding an edge between two vertices would create a cycle

questions.prompt: Why does the height of the structure remain relatively low even after many Union operations are performed?
options: Because the Union by Rank strategy ensures that a smaller tree is always tucked under a larger one, preventing unnecessary height growth.
Because the Find operation's path compression actively moves nodes closer to the root whenever a search is triggered.
Because the Inverse Ackermann function forces the tree to reset its height to zero after a certain number of steps.
Because the structure prevents any node from having more than two children, keeping the tree perfectly balanced.
questions.explanation: While path compression helps, the core reason the height is managed during the 'Union' phase is the Rank heuristic. By attaching the shorter tree to the taller one, the maximum path length from any leaf to the root is minimized.

correctAnswers: Because the Union by Rank strategy ensures that a smaller tree is always tucked under a larger one, preventing unnecessary height growth.

questions.prompt: In the context of the Greedy Choice Property, why is sorting often the first step in the algorithm?
options: To ensure that the problem can be broken down into subproblems.
To organize the data so that the locally optimal choice is always at the front.
To reduce the time complexity from O(n log n) to linear time.
To prove that the problem has an optimal substructure.
questions.explanation: Greedy algorithms rely on making the best immediate choice. Sorting the input according to a specific metric (like value-to-weight ratio) allows the algorithm to quickly access the most 'valuable' local option at each step.
correctAnswers: To organize the data so that the locally optimal choice is always at the front.

questions.prompt: Which of the following conditions must be true for a greedy algorithm to consistently find the globally optimal solution?
options: The Greedy Choice Property: a local optimum leads to a global optimum.
The Optimal Substructure: the optimal solution to the problem contains optimal solutions to subproblems.
The Overlapping Subproblems: subproblems are solved multiple times.
The 'Look-ahead' Property: the algorithm evaluates the impact of current choices on future steps.
questions.explanation: A greedy algorithm is only guaranteed to be optimal if the problem exhibits both the Greedy Choice Property and Optimal Substructure. Overlapping subproblems are a characteristic of Dynamic Programming, and greedy algorithms specifically do not 'look ahead.'
correctAnswers: The Greedy Choice Property: a local optimum leads to a global optimum.
The Optimal Substructure: the optimal solution to the problem contains optimal solutions to subproblems.

questions.prompt: When solving the Fractional Knapsack problem, the most effective greedy metric to sort by is ____.
questions.explanation: By sorting by the ratio of value to weight (density), we ensure we are getting the most 'bang for our buck' for every unit of capacity used in the knapsack.
correctAnswers: value-per-unit-weight
density
value per unit weight
unit value
value/weight ratio

questions.prompt: Why does the greedy approach fail for the 0/1 Knapsack problem but work for the Fractional Knapsack problem?
options: The 0/1 Knapsack problem does not have an optimal substructure.
The fractional version allows for 'perfect' use of capacity, whereas the 0/1 version can leave gaps that local choices can't optimize.
Greedy algorithms are unable to handle integer values.
The 0/1 Knapsack problem requires sorting by weight instead of density.
questions.explanation: In the 0/1 Knapsack, picking the 'best' item can leave just enough space that is too small for the next best items, but which could have been filled more efficiently by two 'lesser' items. The inability to break items means the local choice can lock out a better global combination.
correctAnswers: The fractional version allows for 'perfect' use of capacity, whereas the 0/1 version can leave gaps that local choices can't optimize.

questions.prompt: You are analyzing a recursive function to find the $n^{th}$ value in a sequence. You notice that the same inputs are being recalculated thousands of times across different branches of the recursive tree. Which core property of Dynamic Programming does this situation represent?
options: Optimal Substructure
Overlapping Subproblems
Greedy Choice Property
Iterative Refinement
questions.explanation: Overlapping subproblems occur when a recursive algorithm visits the same problem states multiple times. Dynamic Programming exploits this by storing the result of each subproblem to avoid redundant work.
correctAnswers: Overlapping Subproblems

questions.prompt: A developer is deciding between using a 'top-down' (memoization) approach and a 'bottom-up' (tabulation) approach for a complex optimization problem. What are some typical characteristics of the 'bottom-up' tabulation method?
options: It starts by solving the smallest base cases first.
It generally avoids the risk of recursion stack overflow.
It only computes subproblems that are actually needed for the final solution.
It uses a table-filling approach, usually via iterative loops.
It relies on an 'on-the-fly' cache within a recursive function.
questions.explanation: Tabulation is iterative and starts from the base cases upward, which prevents stack overflow. Unlike memoization (top-down), which may skip unnecessary subproblems, tabulation typically fills the entire table in a predetermined order.
correctAnswers: It starts by solving the smallest base cases first.
It generally avoids the risk of recursion stack overflow.
It uses a table-filling approach, usually via iterative loops.

questions.prompt: The principle that an optimal solution to a large problem can be constructed from the optimal solutions of its smaller subproblems is known as ____.
questions.explanation: Optimal Substructure is the requirement that the global optimum can be defined in terms of local optima of its parts. Without this, DP cannot guarantee a correct final answer.
correctAnswers: Optimal Substructure

questions.prompt: Why is 'Merge Sort' generally not considered a candidate for Dynamic Programming, even though it breaks problems into smaller subproblems?
options: It lacks optimal substructure.
The subproblems are independent and do not overlap.
It cannot be implemented using a bottom-up approach.
The time complexity is already logarithmic.
questions.explanation: In Merge Sort, each sub-array is distinct; there is no 'redundant' work where the same sub-array is sorted multiple times. DP is only useful when subproblems overlap.
correctAnswers: The subproblems are independent and do not overlap.

questions.prompt: As the animation progresses from calculating a small sequence value to a much larger one, why does the 'Top-Down with Memoization' approach stay significantly faster than the 'Plain Recursion' approach?
options: Because memoization converts the branching exponential growth of work into a linear sequence of lookups.
Because the memoization approach skips the base cases entirely to save time.
Because recursive functions are natively faster for computers to execute than loops.
Because the memory table automatically predicts future values without calculating them.
questions.explanation: Plain recursion repeats work for every node in a tree that grows exponentially. Memoization ensures each unique subproblem is computed exactly once, resulting in linear complexity O(n).

questions.prompt: When solving the 0/1 Knapsack problem using a 1D space-optimized array, why is it necessary to iterate through the capacities in reverse (from max capacity down to the item's weight)?
options: To ensure that each item is considered for inclusion at most once by referencing the previous item's state.
To minimize the number of cache misses during the array update process.
Because the base case is always located at the end of the array rather than the beginning.
To allow the algorithm to handle items with negative weights more effectively.
questions.explanation: In the 0/1 Knapsack, if we iterate forward, we might use the 'updated' value of a smaller capacity from the current item's row, effectively allowing the same item to be picked multiple times (the Unbounded Knapsack problem). Iterating backward ensures we only reference values from the previous item's iteration.
correctAnswers: To ensure that each item is considered for inclusion at most once by referencing the previous item's state.

questions.prompt: In the context of the Edit Distance problem (Levenshtein distance) between two strings, which of the following operations correspond correctly to their movement in the DP table?
options: A horizontal move (left to right) represents an insertion.
A vertical move (top to bottom) represents a deletion.
A diagonal move (top-left to bottom-right) always adds a cost of 1.
A diagonal move (top-left to bottom-right) represents a replacement if characters differ.
A vertical move represents a match with zero cost.
questions.explanation: Horizontal moves represent adding a character from the target string (insertion), vertical moves represent skipping a character in the source string (deletion), and diagonal moves represent either a match (cost 0) or a substitution (cost 1).
correctAnswers: A horizontal move (left to right) represents an insertion.
A vertical move (top to bottom) represents a deletion.
A diagonal move (top-left to bottom-right) represents a replacement if characters differ.

questions.prompt: What is the specific 'state' represented by a cell at row 'i' and column 'w' in the standard 0/1 Knapsack DP table?
options: The list of specific item IDs currently inside the bag.
The maximum value achievable using a subset of the first 'i' items with a total weight of exactly 'w'.
The maximum value achievable using a subset of the first 'i' items without exceeding capacity 'w'.
The weight of the heaviest item among the first 'i' items.
questions.explanation: DP states focus on optimization results under constraints. For Knapsack, the state tracks the best value possible given the available items and the remaining weight capacity.
correctAnswers: The maximum value achievable using a subset of the first 'i' items without exceeding capacity 'w'.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are necessary components when defining a Dynamic Programming solution for an optimization problem?
options: Identifying the 'state' which captures the essential constraints.
Defining a recurrence relation to transition between states.
Setting base cases to handle the smallest possible subproblems.
Sorting all input data by value-to-weight ratio to ensure a greedy choice.
Ensuring the problem has the 'overlapping subproblems' property.
questions.explanation: DP requires states, transitions, base cases, and overlapping subproblems. Sorting by ratio is a characteristic of Greedy algorithms, which do not work for 0/1 Knapsack.
correctAnswers: Identifying the 'state' which captures the essential constraints.
Defining a recurrence relation to transition between states.
Setting base cases to handle the smallest possible subproblems.
Ensuring the problem has the 'overlapping subproblems' property.

questions.prompt: In the simulated 0/1 Knapsack table build-up, why do the values in a specific column never decrease as the simulation moves from the top row to the bottom row?
options: Because each new row represents an additional item that can either be ignored or added to increase the previous optimal value.
Because the algorithm sorts items by weight, ensuring that the most valuable items are processed last.
Because the capacity of the knapsack increases linearly as the algorithm iterates through the rows.
Because the 'exclude' path always doubles the value of the cell located directly above it.
questions.explanation: In 0/1 Knapsack, the value for state (i, w) is the max of the value without the item (the cell above) and the value with the item. Since we are taking a maximum, the value can only stay the same or increase as more item options are added.

questions.prompt: You are designing a high-frequency trading engine where decisions must be made in microseconds. A Dynamic Programming approach provides the mathematically optimal result but takes O(N²) time, while a Greedy approach is slightly sub-optimal but runs in O(N). Which factor most justifies choosing the Greedy approach?
options: The problem lacks optimal substructure.
The engineering trade-off prioritizes execution speed over absolute optimality.
Greedy algorithms always provide the global optimum in real-time systems.
The subproblems are independent, making DP unnecessary.
questions.explanation: In real-world engineering, 'best' is context-dependent. A Greedy heuristic is often preferred in time-sensitive systems (like trading or game engines) when the overhead of DP's exhaustive search exceeds the available time budget.
correctAnswers: The engineering trade-off prioritizes execution speed over absolute optimality.

questions.prompt: Which of the following characteristics are 'symptoms' that a problem should be solved using Dynamic Programming rather than Divide and Conquer?
options: The problem can be broken down into smaller subproblems.
Subproblems recur multiple times throughout the execution (overlapping subproblems).
A local choice made now may negatively impact the global optimum later.
The subproblems are entirely independent of one another.
The solution to a subproblem is reused to build the solution to a larger problem.
questions.explanation: While both use subproblems, DP is specifically required when subproblems overlap (reusing results via memoization) and when we must explore multiple paths to ensure a global optimum, unlike DnC where subproblems are independent.
correctAnswers: Subproblems recur multiple times throughout the execution (overlapping subproblems).
A local choice made now may negatively impact the global optimum later.
The solution to a subproblem is reused to build the solution to a larger problem.

questions.prompt: In the 'Greedy Leap' vs. 'DP Safety Net' analogy, a ____ approach is risky because it assumes that the locally optimal choice at each step will lead to the globally optimal solution without looking ahead.
questions.explanation: The 'Greedy Choice Property' assumes that local optimization is sufficient. If this property doesn't hold, the algorithm falls into a 'Greedy Trap' and fails to find the best possible global result.
correctAnswers: Greedy
greedy

questions.prompt: Why is Merge Sort classified as Divide and Conquer, while the 0/1 Knapsack problem is typically solved with Dynamic Programming?
options: Merge Sort subproblems are independent; Knapsack subproblems overlap and require global coordination.
Merge Sort is an optimization problem; Knapsack is a sorting problem.
Merge Sort uses a 'Greedy' choice at each split, whereas Knapsack does not.
Knapsack subproblems are independent, but Merge Sort subproblems overlap.
questions.explanation: In Merge Sort, the two halves of an array do not influence each other's sorting process (independence). In the 0/1 Knapsack problem, the choice to include one item changes the remaining capacity for all subsequent decisions, creating overlapping dependencies.
correctAnswers: Merge Sort subproblems are independent; Knapsack subproblems overlap and require global coordination.

questions.prompt: Watch the pathfinding simulation carefully. Why does the Greedy agent (Red) fail to reach the highest peak while the DP agent (Blue) succeeds?

The Red agent only fails because the subproblems are independent, making Greedy the wrong choice.
The Blue agent uses a heuristic that allows it to ignore parts of the map.
